lesson.title: Shrinking by the Same Percent: Exponential Decay
lesson.summary: Exponential decay describes a quantity that shrinks by the same percentage during each equal time interval, producing a curve that drops quickly at first and then levels off as it approaches zero.
lesson.body:
You already know that exponential growth happens when a quantity is repeatedly multiplied by a factor greater than 1, so it keeps getting bigger and bigger. Exponential decay is the mirror image of that idea. Instead of multiplying by a number greater than 1, you repeatedly multiply by a positive number less than 1, so the quantity keeps getting smaller. A car losing value as it ages, a hot cup of coffee cooling toward room temperature, a dose of medicine leaving the bloodstream, and a radioactive sample breaking down are all real situations that follow this same shrinking pattern.

The general equation for exponential decay looks just like the exponential growth equation you already studied: y equals a times b raised to the power t. Here a is the initial value, the amount you start with before any time has passed, t is the amount of time that has passed, and b is a positive number between 0 and 1. Because b is less than 1, each time t increases by 1, y gets multiplied by a fraction of itself, so it shrinks. It is common to build this equation from a percent decrease: if a quantity loses r percent of itself each period, written as a decimal, then y equals a times the quantity (1 minus r), raised to the power t.

Here is a fully worked example. A car is purchased new for 20,000 dollars, and it loses 15 percent of its value every year. Since r equals 0.15, the equation is y equals 20,000 times (1 minus 0.15) raised to the t, which is y equals 20,000 times 0.85 raised to the t. To find the value after 3 years, compute 0.85 squared first: 0.85 times 0.85 equals 0.7225. Then multiply by 0.85 again: 0.7225 times 0.85 equals 0.614125. Finally multiply by the initial value: 20,000 times 0.614125 equals 12,282.50. So after 3 years the car is worth 12,282.50 dollars. Notice the value did not drop by a third of the original price; it dropped by 15 percent of whatever the car was worth at the start of each year, which is a smaller and smaller dollar amount as the car gets cheaper.

A second common decay pattern is called half-life: the fixed amount of time it takes a quantity to drop to exactly half of its current amount. Suppose a lab starts with an 80 milligram sample of a substance whose half-life is 5 years. After one half-life (5 years), 40 milligrams remain. After two half-lives (10 years), 20 milligrams remain. After three half-lives (15 years), 10 milligrams remain. You can also compute this directly: 80 times (1/2) raised to the 3rd power equals 80 times 0.125, which equals 10 milligrams, matching the step-by-step answer.

Because you are always multiplying by a positive fraction, the quantity in an exponential decay model gets closer and closer to zero but mathematically never actually reaches zero. This matters for how the graph looks, which you will see in a later chapter, and it sets up the next chapter, where the multiplier itself, the number between 0 and 1 that you multiply by each period, gets its own name: the decay factor.
